sections.title: Atom
sections.text: An atom is the smallest unit of an element that takes part in a chemical reaction. Atoms contain protons (positive charge), neutrons (no charge) and electrons (negative charge). Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus; electrons occupy the region around it. For example, a copper wire contains a huge number of copper atoms.

sections.title: Molecule
sections.text: A molecule is a group of two or more atoms chemically bonded together that can exist as a separate unit. H₂ contains two hydrogen atoms; O₂ contains two oxygen atoms; H₂O contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom; CO₂ contains one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms. In a formula, a number written after an element symbol tells how many atoms of that element are present. If no number is written, it means one.

sections.title: Ionic compounds
sections.text: Not every substance consists of separate molecules. Solid sodium chloride (NaCl) forms a repeating arrangement of sodium and chloride ions. NaCl shows the simplest ratio of ions, so it is described as a formula unit rather than a separate molecule.

sections.title: Matter
sections.text: Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. Examples include a book, water, air and a stone. Matter is made of tiny particles such as atoms, molecules or ions.

sections.title: States of matter
sections.text: Solid: particles are close and mainly vibrate around fixed positions, so the solid has a fixed shape and volume. Liquid: particles remain close but move past each other, so a liquid has a fixed volume but takes its container's shape. Gas: particles are far apart and move rapidly, so a gas has no fixed shape or volume and fills its container.

sections.title: Changes of state
sections.text: Melting: solid to liquid, as ice becomes water. Freezing: liquid to solid. Vaporisation: liquid to gas. Condensation: gas to liquid, as vapour forms droplets. Sublimation: solid to gas directly, as dry ice can do under suitable conditions.

sections.title: Pure substances and mixtures
sections.text: A pure substance has a fixed chemical composition. An element contains one kind of atom, e.g. Fe or Cu. A compound contains different elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio, e.g. H₂O or CO₂. A mixture contains substances physically mixed in variable proportions. A homogeneous mixture is uniform throughout, e.g. salt solution or air. A heterogeneous mixture is not uniform, e.g. oil and water.

sections.title: Physical properties
sections.text: Physical properties can be observed or measured without changing the chemical identity of a substance. Examples include colour, density, melting point and boiling point.

sections.title: Chemical properties
sections.text: Chemical properties describe how a substance reacts to form new substances. For example, iron reacts with oxygen and moisture to form rust; wood burns and forms new substances.

sections.title: Measurement
sections.text: A measurement includes a numerical value and a unit. For example, 5 cm means five centimetres. Units make measurements clear and comparable.

sections.title: Seven SI base units
sections.text: Length: metre (m); mass: kilogram (kg); time: second (s); electric current: ampere (A); thermodynamic temperature: kelvin (K); amount of substance: mole (mol); luminous intensity: candela (cd). The SI base unit of mass is kilogram, although grams are common in chemistry.

sections.title: Derived units
sections.text: Derived units combine base units. Area uses m^2; volume uses m^3; speed uses m s^(-1); density uses kg m^(-3); force uses newton (N), equal to kg m s^(-2). Chemistry also commonly uses litres (L), millilitres (mL) and grams (g).

sections.title: Mass and weight
sections.text: Mass measures the amount of matter. Its SI unit is kilogram (kg), though grams (g) are often used in chemistry. Mass does not change when an object moves from Earth to the Moon. Weight is gravitational force: W = m x g, where m is mass and g is gravitational acceleration. Weight is measured in newtons (N) and changes with gravity.

sections.title: Volume
sections.text: Volume is the space occupied by an object or substance. Its SI unit is m^3. Useful conversions: 1 L = 1000 mL; 1 mL = 1 cm^3; 1 L = 1000 cm^3. For a box, volume = length x breadth x height. For an irregular solid that does not dissolve or react in water, the increase in water level after immersion equals its volume.

sections.title: Density
sections.text: Density is mass per unit volume: density = mass / volume. Common units are g cm^(-3), g mL^(-1) and kg m^(-3). Example: mass = 60 g and volume = 20 cm^3. Density = 60 / 20 = 3 g cm^(-3). Rearranging gives mass = density x volume and volume = mass / density.

sections.title: Temperature
sections.text: Temperature indicates how hot or cold something is and is related to the average kinetic energy of its particles. SI unit: kelvin (K). T(K) = t(degrees C) + 273.15; t(degrees C) = T(K) - 273.15. Example: 27 degrees C = 300.15 K, approximately 300 K.

sections.title: Measurement uncertainty
sections.text: No measurement is perfectly exact. Instruments have limited precision. A ruler marked only in centimetres cannot measure a length as finely as a ruler marked in millimetres.

sections.title: Scientific notation
sections.text: Write a number as a x 10^n, where a is at least 1 but less than 10. Large number: 450000 = 4.5 x 10^5. Small number: 0.00072 = 7.2 x 10^(-4). The exponent tells how many places the decimal point moves.

sections.title: Multiplication
sections.text: Multiply the coefficients and add exponents: (2 x 10^3) x (3 x 10^4) = 6 x 10^(3+4) = 6 x 10^7.

sections.title: Division
sections.text: Divide the coefficients and subtract exponents: (8 x 10^7) / (2 x 10^3) = 4 x 10^(7-3) = 4 x 10^4.

sections.title: Addition and subtraction
sections.text: First make the powers of 10 the same. Example: 3 x 10^5 + 2 x 10^4 = 3 x 10^5 + 0.2 x 10^5 = 3.2 x 10^5. Do not add or subtract exponents when adding or subtracting numbers.

sections.title: Rules
sections.text: All non-zero digits count: 347 has 3 significant figures. Zeros between non-zero digits count: 1005 has 4. Leading zeros do not count: 0.0042 has 2. Trailing zeros after a decimal count: 2.500 has 4. Trailing zeros in whole numbers can be ambiguous, so scientific notation can clarify precision: 1.5 x 10^3 has 2 significant figures; 1.500 x 10^3 has 4.

sections.title: Multiplication and division
sections.text: Round the final answer to the same number of significant figures as the input with the fewest. Example: 2.5 x 3.42 = 8.55, which rounds to 8.6 (2 significant figures).

sections.title: Addition and subtraction
sections.text: Round to the least precise decimal place. Example: 12.11 + 3.2 = 15.31, which rounds to 15.3. Keep extra digits in intermediate steps and round at the end.

sections.title: Unit conversion
sections.text: Use a conversion fraction equal to 1, arranged so unwanted units cancel. Example: 2.5 km x (1000 m / 1 km) = 2500 m. Example: 500 mL x (1 L / 1000 mL) = 0.5 L. Check that the final unit matches the requested quantity.

sections.title: Conservation of mass
sections.text: Mass is neither created nor destroyed during an ordinary chemical reaction. In a closed system, total mass of reactants equals total mass of products. Example: 12 g carbon + 32 g oxygen gives 44 g carbon dioxide.

sections.title: Definite proportions
sections.text: A pure compound always contains the same elements in the same fixed proportion by mass. Water has hydrogen and oxygen in a mass ratio of 1:8; 9 g water contains 1 g hydrogen and 8 g oxygen.

sections.title: Multiple proportions
sections.text: When two elements form more than one compound, masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in a simple whole-number ratio. For 12 g carbon, CO contains 16 g oxygen and CO₂ contains 32 g oxygen. Ratio = 1:2.

sections.title: Gay-Lussac's law
sections.text: Reacting gases and gaseous products have simple whole-number volume ratios at the same temperature and pressure. 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) -> 2H₂O(g) has volume ratio 2:1:2 under suitable conditions.

sections.title: Avogadro's law
sections.text: Equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules. At constant temperature and pressure, gas volume is proportional to moles: V is proportional to n.

sections.title: Main ideas
sections.text: Matter is made of atoms. Atoms of different elements have different properties. Compounds form when atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios. Ordinary chemical reactions rearrange atoms rather than creating or destroying them.

sections.title: Modern correction
sections.text: Atoms of the same element can have different masses because of isotopes. Atoms contain protons, neutrons and electrons, so some original statements of Dalton's theory have been revised.

sections.title: Unified atomic mass unit (u or amu)
sections.text: The unified atomic mass unit, symbol u, is exactly one-twelfth of the mass of one carbon-12 atom. It is also commonly called the atomic mass unit (amu). Its approximate value is 1.6605 x 10^(-27) kg. This unit is convenient because atoms are extremely small. Atomic and molecular masses are commonly expressed in u.

sections.title: Atomic mass
sections.text: Atomic mass is the mass of an atom expressed in u. Approximate values: H = 1 u, C = 12 u, N = 14 u, O = 16 u, Na = 23 u and Cl = 35.5 u.

sections.title: Isotopes and average atomic mass
sections.text: Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Average atomic mass is a weighted average: add each isotope's mass multiplied by its fractional abundance. Example: 10 u at 20% and 11 u at 80% gives 10 x 0.20 + 11 x 0.80 = 10.8 u.

sections.title: Molecular mass
sections.text: Add the atomic masses of all atoms in one molecule. H₂O = 2 x 1 + 16 = 18 u. CO₂ = 12 + 2 x 16 = 44 u.

sections.title: Formula mass
sections.text: Add the atomic masses in a formula unit, especially for ionic compounds. NaCl = 23 + 35.5 = 58.5 u.

sections.title: Molar mass difference
sections.text: Atomic or molecular mass is the mass of one atom or molecule in u. Molar mass is the mass of one mole, usually in g mol^(-1). A water molecule has mass about 18 u, while one mole of water has molar mass about 18 g mol^(-1).

sections.title: Why use the mole?
sections.text: Atoms and molecules are too small to count individually in ordinary laboratory work. A mole is a counting unit, just as a dozen means 12 items.

sections.title: Avogadro constant
sections.text: One mole contains exactly 6.02214076 x 10^23 specified entities. School calculations commonly use 6.022 x 10^23. This is the Avogadro constant, N_A. The entities must be specified: atoms, molecules, ions, etc. One mole of O₂ contains 6.022 x 10^23 O₂ molecules, equal to 2 moles of oxygen atoms.

sections.title: Molar mass and formulas
sections.text: Molar mass is the mass of one mole, usually in g mol^(-1). Moles = mass / molar mass. Number of particles = moles x N_A. Moles = number of particles / N_A.

sections.title: Example: moles from mass
sections.text: Find moles in 36 g water. Molar mass H₂O = 18 g mol^(-1). Moles = 36 / 18 = 2 mol.

sections.title: Example: particles from moles
sections.text: Number of molecules in 2 mol water = 2 x 6.022 x 10^23 = 1.2044 x 10^24 molecules.

sections.title: Example: mass from moles
sections.text: Mass of 0.5 mol CO₂ = 0.5 x 44 = 22 g.

sections.title: Formula
sections.text: Percentage by mass of an element = (mass of that element in one mole of compound / molar mass of compound) x 100.

sections.title: Example: water
sections.text: Molar mass H₂O = 18 g mol^(-1). Hydrogen percentage = (2/18) x 100 = 11.11%. Oxygen percentage = (16/18) x 100 = 88.89%. Total = 100%.

sections.title: Empirical formula
sections.text: The empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms. C₆H₁₂O₆ simplifies to CH₂O; H₂O₂ simplifies to HO.

sections.title: Finding empirical formula
sections.text: Assume 100 g if percentages are given, so percentages become grams. Divide each mass by its atomic mass to find moles. Divide all mole values by the smallest. Convert the ratios to whole numbers; multiply all ratios by a small integer if necessary.

sections.title: Example
sections.text: A compound has 40% C, 6.67% H and 53.33% O. In 100 g: C = 40/12 = about 3.33 mol; H = 6.67/1 = 6.67 mol; O = 53.33/16 = about 3.33 mol. Divide by 3.33 to get 1:2:1. Empirical formula = CH₂O.

sections.title: Molecular formula
sections.text: Molecular formula gives the actual number of atoms in a molecule. Multiplier n = molecular molar mass / empirical formula mass. Multiply each empirical-formula subscript by n. Example: CH₂O has formula mass 30. If molecular molar mass is 180, n = 180/30 = 6, so molecular formula = C₆H₁₂O₆.

sections.title: Stoichiometry
sections.text: Stoichiometry calculates the amounts of reactants and products using a balanced chemical equation.

sections.title: Balanced equations
sections.text: A balanced equation has equal numbers of each element's atoms on both sides. 2H₂ + O₂ -> 2H₂O has 4 H atoms and 2 O atoms on each side. Coefficients give the mole ratio 2:1:2. Change coefficients, never subscripts, to balance equations.

sections.title: Calculation steps
sections.text: 1. Balance the equation. 2. Convert the known mass to moles. 3. Use the coefficient ratio. 4. Convert required moles to mass if needed. 5. Include units.

sections.title: Example
sections.text: 4 g H₂ = 4/2 = 2 mol H₂. With excess oxygen, the H₂:H₂O ratio is 1:1, so 2 mol water forms. Mass = 2 x 18 = 36 g, assuming complete reaction.

sections.title: Limiting reagent
sections.text: The limiting reagent is used up first and limits the amount of product. The excess reagent remains. For 2H₂ + O₂ -> 2H₂O, 4 mol H₂ and 1 mol O₂ make 2 mol H₂O; O₂ is limiting and 2 mol H₂ remain.

sections.title: Solution, solute and solvent
sections.text: A solution is a homogeneous mixture. The solute is the substance dissolved; the solvent does the dissolving. In salt water, salt is solute and water is solvent.

sections.title: Mass percent
sections.text: Mass % = (mass of solute / mass of solution) x 100. Mass of solution = mass of solute + mass of solvent. Example: 10 g salt + 90 g water gives 100 g solution, so salt mass percent = 10%.

sections.title: Mole fraction
sections.text: Mole fraction of A = moles of A / total moles. For A and B: X_A = n_A/(n_A+n_B); X_B = n_B/(n_A+n_B). All mole fractions add to 1. Example: 2 mol A and 3 mol B gives X_A = 0.4 and X_B = 0.6. Mole fraction has no unit.

sections.title: Molarity
sections.text: Molarity = moles of solute / volume of solution in litres. Unit: mol L^(-1), also written M. Example: 0.5 mol in 250 mL solution; 250 mL = 0.250 L, so molarity = 0.5/0.250 = 2 mol L^(-1). Use solution volume, not solvent volume. Molarity can change with temperature.

sections.title: Molality
sections.text: Molality = moles of solute / mass of solvent in kg. Unit: mol kg^(-1). Example: 0.5 mol solute in 250 g = 0.250 kg solvent gives molality = 0.5/0.250 = 2 mol kg^(-1). Use solvent mass, not solution mass. Molality does not change with temperature.

sections.title: Molarity versus molality
sections.text: Molarity uses volume of solution and may change with temperature. Molality uses mass of solvent and does not change with temperature.

sections.title: Core formulas
sections.text: Density = mass / volume. Weight = mass x gravitational acceleration. T(K) = t(degrees C) + 273.15. Moles = mass / molar mass. Particles = moles x Avogadro constant. Percentage composition = (mass of element / mass of compound) x 100. Molecular-formula multiplier = molecular molar mass / empirical formula mass. Mass % = (mass of solute / mass of solution) x 100. Mole fraction = moles of component / total moles. Molarity = moles of solute / litres of solution. Molality = moles of solute / kg of solvent.

sections.title: Common distinctions
sections.text: Mass vs weight: amount of matter vs gravitational force. Atomic/molecular mass uses u; molar mass uses g mol^(-1). Empirical formula gives the simplest ratio; molecular formula gives actual atom counts. Limiting reagent runs out first. Molarity uses solution volume; molality uses solvent mass. Multiplication/division use significant figures; addition/subtraction use decimal-place precision.
